text: You just saw how Azure builds a landing zone out of management groups, platform subscriptions, and subscription vending. This lesson names AWS's answer to the exact same problem — Organizations, Control Tower, and Account Factory — using different vocabulary for a structure you'll recognize immediately.

Where Azure groups subscriptions under management groups, AWS groups accounts under Organizational Units inside AWS Organizations. The shape is the same idea: a root, OUs nested beneath it, accounts placed inside OUs, and policy attached at an OU level inherited by every account under it. An AWS account is a harder isolation boundary than an Azure subscription — most resources and service limits are fully contained within one account — which is exactly why this matters as much on AWS as management group design does on Azure.

AWS Control Tower stands up that structure in one guided setup rather than assembling it by hand. The first time it's enabled, it creates a Management account used only for billing and administration, a dedicated Log Archive account that receives CloudTrail and Config data from every account in the organization, and a separate Audit account with read access across the org for security tooling — logs and audit tooling isolated from workload accounts, the same decision Azure's Platform subscriptions made.

Control Tower enforces that structure with two kinds of guardrail. Preventive guardrails are Service Control Policies, attached at the OU level, that deny an API call outright regardless of what any IAM policy inside the account allows — SCPs sit above IAM, not alongside it. Detective guardrails are AWS Config rules that continuously evaluate existing resources and flag drift after the fact, without blocking it. Together they stop what can be stopped and catch what can't.

Account Factory is Control Tower's version of subscription vending: a standardized way to provision a new account that's already in the right OU, already guardrailed, and already logging to the Log Archive account. Account Factory for Terraform, AFT, does the same thing driven entirely by Terraform configuration — the direct AWS counterpart to the vending module from last lesson, built on the same Course 8 skills.

You now know how both clouds build the boundary structure itself — management groups and OUs, platform and security accounts, vending and Account Factory. Next lesson asks the harder question neither vendor answers for you: where should those boundaries actually go, and why blast radius beats the org chart as the deciding factor.
